# HIE-CM m1 build

Scaffolds an ABDM m1 integration one journey at a time. It covers ABHA creation, login and profile management.

## How this skill runs

Every journey below is an OODA loop, not a recipe: observe the actual state (last response, last error), orient against the step matched below, decide the cheapest next action, act, and return to observe. A step is done only when its exit condition is observed against the sandbox, never because it "should have worked."

Loop limit: 8 passes per step. Hitting the limit is an escalation: state what was observed, what was tried, and which operation page to read, then ask one question.

## Before the first journey, when the codebase already exists

Skip this section only for a system that does not exist yet. Otherwise it runs first, and its exit condition is a written plan, not a call.

### In plain words

Most ABDM integrations are not new systems. They are a hospital management
system, a laboratory system or a clinic application that already has patients,
visits, records, a login, an HTTP client and a way of keeping secrets. Every
ABDM journey has to land somewhere inside that, and a journey built before the
codebase has been read lands in the wrong place: a second HTTP client beside the
first, an ABHA column on the wrong table, a callback route the reverse proxy
never forwards.

So the first loop is not a journey. It is a survey of the system as it is, and
its exit condition is a written plan that names, for every ABDM touchpoint, the
file it will live in. The journeys then build against that plan rather than
against the specification's idea of a fresh codebase.

### Before you start

- The repository, checked out, with permission to read all of it. A survey of
  half a codebase produces a plan for half a system.
- The answers to the deployment interview. The
  code says what the system is. Only the integrator can say what the
  deployment is, and the two together decide which journeys are built at all.
- The practices that hold across every call, which
  the plan has to leave room for.

### What happens

This is one loop with a limit of eight passes over the codebase. Each pass
reads live state only, which here means the files themselves, never a README's
description of them and never an assumption carried from a similar system.

**Observe.** Inventory the system from its manifests and its tree, not from its
documentation. Record file paths for each of these, or record that none exists:

| Find | Where it usually shows | Why ABDM needs it |
|---|---|---|
| Languages and runtime versions | package manifests, lock files, toolchain files | Every generated call has to be idiomatic here |
| Build, run and test commands | manifests, CI configuration, a Makefile | Each journey's exit condition becomes a test that runs the same way |
| The frontend and backend split, and how they talk | the top level tree, an API client in the frontend, route definitions in the backend | The counter screens go in the frontend; every ABDM call goes through the backend |
| The outbound HTTP client the backend already uses | the dependency list, a shared client module | ABDM calls reuse it, or a second one appears and the two drift |
| How secrets and configuration reach the process | environment loading, a vault client, a config file | The client id, the secret and the access token travel the same way |
| The patient model, and the identifier fields it already carries | the schema, the ORM models, the migrations | The ABHA number and address become columns beside the existing identifiers, not a new table |
| The visit, encounter or record model | the same places | A care context maps to one of these, and the plan has to say which |
| Where inbound HTTP is routed and authenticated, and whether the deployment has a public URL | the router, the middleware, the reverse proxy configuration, the deployment manifests | ABDM calls back, and a callback route that nothing forwards is silence nobody notices |
| Existing cryptography helpers | a security or crypto module, the dependency list | The RSA encryption of identifiers reuses them |
| Where errors are shown to a user, and where they are logged | the frontend's error surface, the logging setup | A refused call has to land on the screen the person is looking at, and never log a token |

**Orient.** Map each ABDM touchpoint onto that inventory. Where the map is
exact, write the file path. Where it is not, write two candidates and say what
would decide between them. The common ambiguities: two places that could hold
the patient identifier, an HTTP client in the frontend and none in the backend,
a monorepo with several services and no obvious owner for callbacks.

Then read the interview answers against the inventory. A government integrator
gets the demographic route; a facility with no public URL gets no callback
driven journey until it has one; a desk with a fingerprint reader gets the
biometric method. The route set is the intersection of what the deployment
allows and what the code can host.

**Decide.** Order the journeys. The token comes first because every other call
needs it: the gateway session token, or for M4 the bearer token the registry calls
carry. Then the journey whose exit condition can be observed with
the least new code, usually a profile read for a patient who already holds an
ABHA. Creation and linking come after, because each depends on state the earlier
ones produce. For each journey, name the files it will touch and the test that
proves its exit condition.

**Act.** Write the plan. It is a file in the repository, at the path the
integrator names or at the root as `abdm-integration-plan.md`, and it is the
only output of this loop. Then return to observe once, reading the plan against
the tree, to confirm every path in it exists or is marked as new.

If the limit is reached with questions still open, escalate: name what was
found, name the two candidates that could not be separated, point at this
atom, and ask one question.

### How you know it worked

The plan exists and answers every row of the inventory table with a file path,
or with the words none, add at, followed by a path. No row is blank and no row
says to be decided.

Every ABDM touchpoint in the plan names one file, or names two candidates and
the observation that would choose between them. Every journey in the plan names
the test that proves its exit condition and the command that runs it.

Open the plan beside the tree. Every path it names resolves, or is marked as
new. That is the observation that ends this loop, and the first journey does
not start until it has been made.

### When it goes wrong

- **The plan puts the HTTP client in the frontend.** The survey found the
  frontend's API client and stopped. Every ABDM call carries a secret, so it
  goes through the backend, and the plan has to say which backend module.
- **Two patient tables, and the plan picked one.** Orient produced one
  hypothesis where it needed two. Name both, and name the query that shows
  which one the visit model points at.
- **The plan has a callback route and the deployment has no public URL.** The
  inventory row on inbound routing was answered from the router rather than
  from the deployment. Mark every callback driven journey as blocked on a URL,
  and build the ones that are not.
- **The survey read the README and not the tree.** A README describes the
  system somebody meant to build. The plan is for the one that exists.
- **Eight passes and the plan is still incomplete.** Escalate with the rows
  that are answered, the rows that are not, this atom, and one question about
  the row that blocks the most journeys.

**Act: the calls in this journey, in order**

#### 1. Send Aadhaar OTP for ABHA enrolment (`m1_post_v3_enrollment_request_otp_aadhaar_otp`)

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/request/otp \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "txnId": "{{txnId}}",
  "scope": [
    "abha-enrol"
  ],
  "loginHint": "aadhaar",
  "loginId": "{{encrypted aadhaar number}}",
  "otpSystem": "aadhaar"
}'
```

#### 2. Create ABHA - verify Aadhaar OTP (`m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_byaadhaar_otp`)

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/enrol/byAadhaar \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'BENEFIT_NAME: {{Benefit Name}}' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "authData": {
    "authMethods": [
      "otp"
    ],
    "otp": {
      "txnId": "{{txnId}}",
      "otpValue": "{{encrypted otp}}",
      "mobile": "{{mobile number}}"
    }
  },
  "consent": {
    "code": "abha-enrollment",
    "version": "1.4"
  }
}'
```

#### 3. After ABHA creation - send OTP to verify mobile (optional) (`m1_post_v3_enrollment_request_otp_mobile_verify_create_ab_1b66bb`)

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/request/otp \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "txnId": "{{txnId}}",
  "scope": [
    "abha-enrol",
    "mobile-verify"
  ],
  "loginHint": "mobile",
  "loginId": "{{encrypted mobileNumber}}",
  "otpSystem": "abdm"
}'
```

#### 4. After ABHA creation - verify mobile OTP (optional) (`m1_post_v3_enrollment_auth_byabdm_mobile_verify_create_ab_091285`)

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/auth/byAbdm \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "scope": [
    "abha-enrol",
    "mobile-verify"
  ],
  "authData": {
    "authMethods": [
      "otp"
    ],
    "otp": {
      "txnId": "{{txnId}}",
      "otpValue": "{{encrypted otp}}"
    }
  }
}'
```

#### 5. After ABHA creation - send OTP to verify email (optional) (`m1_post_v3_enrollment_request_otp_email_verify_create_abh_ddbed1`)

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/request/otp \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "txnId": "{{txnId}}",
  "scope": [
    "abha-enrol",
    "email-verify"
  ],
  "loginHint": "email",
  "loginId": "{{encrypted email}}",
  "otpSystem": "abdm"
}'
```

#### 6. After ABHA creation - verify email OTP (optional) (`m1_post_v3_enrollment_auth_byabdm_email_verify_create_abh_6d732c`)

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/auth/byAbdm \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "scope": [
    "abha-enrol",
    "email-verify"
  ],
  "authData": {
    "authMethods": [
      "otp"
    ],
    "otp": {
      "txnId": "{{txnId}}",
      "otpValue": "{{encrypted otp}}"
    }
  }
}'
```

#### 7. After ABHA creation - get ABHA address suggestions (`m1_get_v3_enrollment_enrol_suggestion_create_abha_aadhaar_otp`)

```bash
curl --request GET \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/enrol/suggestion \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'TRANSACTION_ID: {{txnId}}' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z'
```

#### 8. After ABHA creation - create ABHA address (`m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_abha_address_create_abha_aadhaar_otp`)

```bash
curl --request POST \
  --url https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api/v3/enrollment/enrol/abha-address \
  --header 'Authorization: ******' \
  --header 'REQUEST-ID: 18235d89-cb13-479d-ad71-7a57d5f669a8' \
  --header 'TIMESTAMP: 2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z' \
  --header 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{
  "txnId": "{{txnId}}",
  "abhaAddress": "{{ABHA Address}}",
  "preferred": 1
}'
```

**Exit condition (Observe until this is true)**

A 200 whose body matches:

```json
{
  "txnId": "23acf181-339d-4771-b532-5c5df4a28d19",
  "healthIdNumber": "<ABHA_NUMBER>",
  "preferredAbhaAddress": "<ABHA_ADDRESS>"
}
```

The ids, the mandatory marks and the wording of each check are ABDM's, from the M1 ABHA creation and verification set. The sections are grouped as the set groups them. Where the set names an operation, the operation id here is the one in `references/integrate.md`, which carries the host, the headers and a full request.

### CRT_ABHA_101 to 115: create an ABHA by Aadhaar OTP

Applies to every integrator. Mandatory unless marked. This is the group every other creation group repeats with a different authentication step, so it is written in full and the others state only what differs.

Loop limit: 3 passes per test case.

**Preconditions.** A gateway access token less than 30 minutes old. A person present with an Aadhaar linked mobile. Their Aadhaar number searched first on the login path and not found, so the run creates rather than duplicates.

#### CRT_ABHA_101, the option exists. `sandbox`

Your system offers ABHA creation by Aadhaar OTP, and the journey completes. Drive it end to end through your screen or API.

Calls, in order: `m1_post_v3_enrollment_request_otp_aadhaar_otp`, `m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_byaadhaar_otp`, the optional mobile and email verifications, `m1_get_v3_enrollment_enrol_suggestion_create_abha_aadhaar_otp`, `m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_abha_address_create_abha_aadhaar_otp`, then `m1_get_v3_profile_account` and `m1_get_v3_profile_account_abha_card`.

Exit condition: three literals, all pasted.

1. `m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_byaadhaar_otp` returns 200 with `tokens.token` present and `ABHAProfile.ABHANumber` present.
2. `m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_abha_address_create_abha_aadhaar_otp` returns 200 with `healthIdNumber` and `preferredAbhaAddress`.
3. `m1_get_v3_profile_account`, sent with that `X-token`, returns 200 with the same `ABHANumber`.

Nudge: read `message` on step 1. `Account created successfully` is a new account. `This account already exist` is a 200 too, and it means the search-first rule was skipped or the sandbox person already holds one. Record which, because the second is a screen failure on CRT_ABHA_101 even though the API passed.

#### CRT_ABHA_102, consent is shown and recorded. `screen`

Your system shows the published ABDM consent text before the Aadhaar number is asked for, and stores that the person agreed, with when. Evidence: the consent screen, and the stored record for this run. `hiecm.concept.m1-screen-contract`

#### CRT_ABHA_103, consent in another language. `screen`, optional

The same consent offered in at least one language other than English. Evidence: the screen in that language. Record `not-run` if you do not claim it.

#### CRT_ABHA_104, an invalid Aadhaar number is refused before any call. `screen`

Enter an 11 digit and a 13 digit value. Your system refuses each with a message that says the number is not valid, and sends nothing. Evidence: the refusal on screen and an empty call log for that attempt. Your own check has to be the strict one here; the sandbox's refusal for a bad number is not the one this case is about. `hiecm.concept.m1-honest-screen-states`

#### CRT_ABHA_105, the Aadhaar OTP is requested and can be entered. `sandbox`, then `human`

Exit condition: `m1_post_v3_enrollment_request_otp_aadhaar_otp` returns 200 with a `txnId` and a `message` that names the masked mobile. Paste it. Then stop: the OTP arrives on the person's phone and only they enter it. If they are not there, record `needs-human` and the txnId, and do not mark the case passed or failed.

Screen check alongside: the prompt tells the person the OTP went to the mobile linked with Aadhaar and shows the last digits, which the `message` carries.

#### CRT_ABHA_106, resend OTP. `screen`

The resend control is disabled for 60 seconds after each send and works at most twice. Evidence: a recording or three timestamped screenshots: disabled at send, enabled after 60 seconds, disabled after the second resend. A resend that works reuses the `txnId`; a fresh `txnId` is a new request, not a resend.

#### CRT_ABHA_107, the OTP is verified, and a wrong OTP is refused. `sandbox`, `human`

Two observations, both needed.

1. A wrong OTP: `m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_byaadhaar_otp` returns 422 with `error.code` `ABDM-1204` and a message naming an invalid Aadhaar OTP value, and your screen says the OTP was wrong and lets the person retry without re-entering the Aadhaar number.
2. The right OTP: the 200 from CRT_ABHA_101 step 1.

The person enters both OTPs. Stop for each.

#### CRT_ABHA_108, the communication mobile is the Aadhaar mobile. `sandbox`, optional

If your system checks whether the mobile the person gave is the Aadhaar linked one and skips the second OTP when it is, drive that path. Exit condition: the journey reaches the ABHA address step with no `mobile-verify` call in the log. Record `not-run` if you always verify, which CRT_ABHA_109 then covers.

#### CRT_ABHA_109, a different communication mobile is verified. `sandbox`, `human`

Give a mobile that is not the Aadhaar linked one. Exit condition: `m1_post_v3_enrollment_request_otp_mobile_verify_create_ab_1b66bb` returns 200 with a `txnId`, the person enters the OTP, and `m1_post_v3_enrollment_auth_byabdm_mobile_verify_create_ab_091285` returns 200. A wrong OTP here is refused on screen and the person can retry.

#### CRT_ABHA_112, the ABHA address is suggested and validated. `sandbox` and `screen`

Mandatory for private and government integrators. Optional for a programme that creates a default address by demographic authentication.

Exit condition: `m1_get_v3_enrollment_enrol_suggestion_create_abha_aadhaar_otp` returns 200 with `abhaAddressList` holding at least three entries, and `m1_post_v3_enrollment_enrol_abha_address_create_abha_aadhaar_otp` returns 200 with `preferredAbhaAddress` equal to the one chosen.

Screen check: at least three suggestions are shown, or a free field with these rules printed beside it, and an address already taken is refused with a message that says so and offers the suggestions.

```text
length 8 to 18
letters, digits, or both
at most one dot and at most one underscore, neither first nor last
```

#### CRT_ABHA_113, the ABHA number is displayed. `screen`

The 14 digit ABHA number and the ABHA address from CRT_ABHA_112 are shown together after creation. Evidence: the screen, with the number matching `healthIdNumber` from the pasted response.

#### CRT_ABHA_114, the ABHA card can be viewed and downloaded. `sandbox` and `screen`

Mandatory for private integrators that generate the card. Exit condition: `m1_get_v3_profile_account_abha_card` returns 200 with content type `image/png`, sent with the `X-token` from creation. Screen check: the card shown carries the ABHA number, the QR code, date of birth, gender and the ABHA address. The photo is optional.

#### CRT_ABHA_115, your own card carries the ABHA details. `screen`

For an integrator that prints its own programme card instead. Mandatory for government where CRT_ABHA_114 is not done. The card shows the ABHA number and address, and your system stores both against your own patient id. Evidence: the card and the stored record.

### CRT_ABHA_201 to 210: create an ABHA by Aadhaar biometric

Applies to every integrator. Optional, except that CRT_ABHA_209 is mandatory for a private integrator that generates the card and one of 209 or 210 is mandatory for government.

- Read their profile, which carries the whole registration form: names, date of birth, gender, mobile, address with its codes, and a photograph.
- Find an ABHA somebody has forgotten, and pick the right account when one mobile holds several.
- Show the ABHA card and QR code, and take a profile a patient shares by QR at your counter.
- Update a profile and change a mobile.

What it cannot do yet matters as much. Read **Before anything else** below before assuming a capability is one endpoint away.

## Before anything else

- Treat every request and response shape in this skill as unconfirmed until the sandbox has answered you. Check a response before you rely on its shape.
- The design section is different in kind. Its rules come from building a working front desk against the sandbox, and each atom it cites names what was observed and the date it was seen.
- ABDM publishes operations, not a user experience. The journey is the integrator's to design, so offer the shape below as a suggestion and build what they ask for instead when they have a view of their own counter.
- The ABHA step comes before the registration form and fills it. A verified profile carries the whole form, so a journey that registers the patient first and offers ABHA afterwards has already spent the keystrokes it existed to save.
- Two ways the profile reaches the desk. The patient scans a QR and consents in their own app, and ABDM posts the profile to your callback, so nobody types or asks anything. Or the desk runs the identifier journey. The filled form is the destination either way.
- Decide deliberately whether a journey can complete without an ABHA. A record keyed by the facility's own number does not need one, and a journey that cannot finish without one blocks care for anyone who has none.
- An identifier and an auth method are two different questions, and listing them together is what makes M1 look like five choices. Ask which identifier first, then offer auth methods underneath it, and only where there is more than one.
- Every identifier starts on the login path, Aadhaar included. A verified login already returns the accounts, and only ABDM-1114 on a refusal means nobody holds one. Create on any other answer and the patient ends up with two numbers, which nothing merges.
- Get an access token first, from the gateway session endpoint. Every other call needs it in `Authorization: ******
- Two tokens exist and they are not interchangeable. The gateway access token goes in `Authorization`. The user token from an enrolment or a login goes in `X-token`. Profile endpoints need both.
- Sensitive fields travel encrypted. Aadhaar numbers, mobile numbers, email addresses, OTP values and passwords are encrypted before they go in the body, then base64 encoded.
- The certificate response tells you the padding. `GET /v3/profile/public/certificate` returns `{"publicKey", "encryptionAlgorithm"}`. Read that field and translate it for your language. Do not hard code a padding: a constant is right until it is not, and the failure then looks like a bad value rather than a stale constant.
- One path serves several jobs. The `scope` array in the body picks which one, so read it before assuming an endpoint does one thing.
- The accounts array on a login verification already carries ABHANumber, preferredAbhaAddress, name, gender, dob, profilePhoto and kycVerified, so a registration form can fill the moment the OTP verifies and before any profile call.

## Practices that hold across every call

- Read the body, not only the status. A refusal often names the field in its body while the status says nothing useful.
- When ABDM publishes a value, read it rather than hard coding what it currently says. That covers a parameter, such as the encryption algorithm the certificate endpoints return beside the key, and it covers an enumeration. The registries publish theirs as master data calls: councils, courses, colleges, states and districts on the HPR, and facility types and LGD codes on the HFR. A table typed into your source goes stale silently. Purposes and HI types have no master data call: take them from the enumeration in the specification of the call you are making. Refuse to act on a published value you do not recognise rather than falling back to a default.
- Read every field in a response, not the one you came for. The M1 certificate call returns the encryption algorithm next to the key.
- Prove an assumption against a call that is able to disagree with you. A call that refuses every input with one message cannot tell you which input was right.
- Suspect the transport before the data. When a call refuses a value you believe in, check the encryption, the headers and the clock before you doubt the value.
- Do not carry an encryption path from one module to another. Read the certificate and the algorithm from the registry you are calling.
- Never log a sensitive value before you encrypt it, and never send one to a remote service to be encrypted. Both move the leak rather than removing it.
- Generate a fresh REQUEST-ID for every call and log it before sending. Once a call has failed it is the only handle on it.
- Check the host on any sample before you copy it. A request copied whole can be correct in every respect except where it is pointed, and that failure looks like credentials.
- Do not validate an identifier more strictly than the platform does. A schema that types a field as a UUID is not a promise that every value is one. Refusing a value ABDM would have accepted turns your own client into the thing that broke.
- Read a plural response as plural. A verification returns an accounts array and a consent request can produce more than one artefact. Store the collection and decide from its length.
- A documented callback path is not a documented callback payload. Log the whole body on arrival before you parse it, so a handler written against an assumed shape fails where you can see it.
- Decode a token before you use it. A call that hands you a token has not necessarily handed you the token the next call wants, and the claims are base64 that need no library to read.
- When a journey carries the same parameter through two calls, check what each call's specification asks for rather than carrying the first value forward.
- Do not infer which path an identifier belongs to from where that identifier is most discussed. Send every identifier to the lookup first and let the answer pick the path, so nobody who already holds an account is sent to create a second.
- Do not match an error code with string equality. A code may come back bare, as `ABDM-1001`, or with a trailing `: ` separator, as `ABDM-1001: `. Match on the code itself and tolerate the separator.
- Handle a failure that carries no body. Check for an empty body before you parse, or your client throws on the simplest failure there is.
- Back off on an authentication failure rather than retrying, and never loop a credential check.
- Send TIMESTAMP in UTC, ISO-8601 with milliseconds and a trailing Z, as in `2022-10-06T15:10:00.587Z`.
- Cache a public certificate with a validity window rather than forever. A rotation fails every encrypted call at once, and a cache with no expiry cannot recover on its own.

Demographic authentication is one call and spends no one time password. A
government integrator is required to offer it and a private integrator is not
asked for it, so most integrators build the five call route instead, because it
is the one the specification leads with.

The cheapest journey involves no desk call at all. A registered facility with a
callback ABDM can reach can put a QR code at the counter, and the profile
arrives already consented.

Some lookups cost nothing. A login attempt on an identifier nobody holds is
refused `ABDM-1114` before any one time password is sent, so looking before
creating is free for exactly the people you would otherwise send to create a
duplicate.

### How you know it worked

A receptionist registering a patient who brought an ABHA types corrections only.
Every field the profile carries arrives filled, and the only screen asking for
input is the one confirming the form.


It is caused by journey decisions rather than by any single call. Four of them
matter.

### What happens

**Every identifier starts on the login path, Aadhaar included.** Wiring Aadhaar
straight to enrolment, because enrolment is where Aadhaar is most discussed,
sends everybody who already holds an ABHA to make a second one.

**`ABDM-1114` is the only answer that means nobody holds an ABHA.** A refusal
that names a field is not the same thing. A stale certificate reads back
identically, and creating an account on that is how the duplicate happens.

**Never ask the patient whether they want to log in or to create.** They often
cannot answer. One screen, titled for both outcomes, takes an identifier and
lets the response decide.

**Read the token, not the account count.** A verification that returns a
`refreshToken` has already returned the final user token, so use it. One without
a `refreshToken` is a short lived transfer token and must be exchanged at the
account selection call, whatever the length of the accounts array. Branching on
`accounts.length` sends the Aadhaar path into an exchange it must not make, and
the refusal then blames the token's shape rather than saying the call was
unnecessary.

Creation is from Aadhaar. ABDM publishes a mobile enrolment route, and an
account created that way is address only and never verified against a
government identity document. No later desk can look it up before spending a one
time password, and the person carries the lesser account permanently. Write that
rule into code as a guard that refuses an unknown method by name, because a rule
the code merely happens to satisfy is one that regresses silently.

When the desk already knows there is no ABHA, ask only for Aadhaar. Offering a
mobile there offers a path that cannot finish. The lookup still runs first: a
patient saying they have never had one is not evidence, and creating on somebody's
word is how the second number appears.

### How you know it worked

Run a login for an identifier nobody holds. You receive `404` with `ABDM-1114`,
no one time password is sent, and only then does the journey offer creation.

Run the Aadhaar login path. The verify response carries a `refreshToken`, the
journey uses it directly, and no exchange call is made. Run the mobile path and
the exchange call is made, because no `refreshToken` came back.

### When it goes wrong

- A login is refused with a message naming a field, and the journey offers
  creation anyway. Only `ABDM-1114` means nobody holds an account. Treat
  anything else as a failure to answer the question.
- The Aadhaar path is refused `Invalid T-token` at the account selection call.
  The journey branched on the account count instead of on `refreshToken`, and
  made a call it did not need to make.

I'm confirming the token header format uses Bearer-style values, then checking the login verify response shape—specifically how the authResult field signals failure, since I need to raise an error when it comes back as "failed".

Now I'm turning to the backend design, starting with the transaction model that tracks flow state—fields like user, flow type, identifier type, login family, OTP system, encrypted login identifier, ABDM transaction ID, pending step, resend count, tokens, and expiry.

Still defining transaction model fields...

I'm reasoning through PII handling: whether to store the plain mobile number versus a ciphertext. Since mobile is sent plain in the Aadhaar enrollment verify-OTP body, I only need it transiently at that request, but for supporting a later mobile-verify resend, I decide to store an encrypted mobile ciphertext captured during the enrol-verify step instead of keeping plaintext around.

I'm also considering whether the person should be allowed to change the mobile number at the send_mobile_otp step — simplest approach is to accept an optional mobile parameter there, encrypting and using it if provided, otherwise falling back to the stored ciphertext. Tokens themselves live server-side in a Redis cache, with the X-token cache TTL set to match its 1800-second expiry.

Now I'm starting to lay out the actual backend endpoints and their request/response contracts for each flow.

I'm defining a shared response shape across these journey endpoints — one that carries the transaction id, current step (otp, choose_account, not_found, mobile_verify, address, verified), optional messages, masked mobile number, which OTP system was used, resend timing info, account list, ABHA address suggestions, profile data once verified, linked patient info, and a flag indicating if the user is new.

Now I'm sketching a helper function that builds this state dict from a transaction object plus extra fields, then outlining the actual endpoint list starting with status check and the login OTP-send endpoint.

For that OTP-send endpoint, I need to handle each identifier type differently: aadhaar requires 12-digit validation and encryption before requesting OTP with aadhaar-verify scope; mobile needs 10-digit validation with abdm otpSystem; abha_number needs 14-digit validation (normalizing hyphens) and lets the user pick between Aadhaar or Mobile OTP; abha_address assumes the frontend already searched, so this just requests OTP via the PHR family with either otp system.

I'm also thinking through how to handle the ABDM-1114 "not found" error for different identifier types — for aadhaar it should allow account creation by holding the ciphertext in a transaction, for mobile it should prompt the user for their Aadhaar number since mobile alone can't create an account, and for abha_number it shouldn't normally hit this case since those are pre-existing identifiers.

Then I'm moving to the success path: storing the transaction ID and pending login step, tracking OTP sent time and resend count, and responding with the masked mobile number and resend details. Next I need to design the verify_otp endpoint that takes the transaction ID and OTP code.

For the verify_otp flow, I'm working out the branching logic: if the auth result includes a refresh token, I use it to fetch the profile directly via X-token; otherwise I check the T-token's accounts list — a single account auto-verifies, multiple accounts triggers a "choose_account" step with sanitized account data, and zero accounts returns "not_found" with create-allowed flags for aadhaar/mobile flows. Now I'm considering how this differs for Aadhaar-based logins specifically.

For the PHR address login path, the token from phr_login_verify is used directly as the X-token, and I fetch the profile through the PHR-specific endpoint since there's typically just one user entry. Once verified across any of these paths, I'm normalizing the profile data into a common AbhaProfile shape with fields like abha_number, abha_address, name components, gender, and date of birth.

I still need fields for year_of_birth, mobile, address/district/state/pincode, photo, kyc_verified, and status. I also want to check for a linked patient via abha_number or abha_address and return just id and name for dedupe purposes -- this seems acceptable since the patient detail page itself has its own permission checks.

Next, the verify_user endpoint takes a transaction_id and abha_number, validates it's one of the transaction's accounts, and proceeds through the T-token to X-token to profile flow to confirm verification.

Then I'm designing the abha_address search endpoint: normalize the address by appending the suffix if missing, search via phr, and return address, auth methods, blocked methods, name, masked mobile, and status. For the not-found case (ABDM-1211), I'm deciding whether to return a 200 with found:false or raise an error -- I think returning a 400 with the ABDM-1211 code tied to the abha_address field is cleaner, since the frontend can treat it as an inline validation error.

I also need to filter auth methods to what this desk supports: AADHAAR_OTP maps to the aadhaar otp_system, MOBILE_OTP maps to abdm, while demographics, Aadhaar biometric, and password aren't supported here.

Moving to the create/send_otp endpoint, I'm working through requiring consent agreement (raising CRT_ABHA_102 if missing), recording an AbhaConsent record with creator, facility, and language, then handling the Aadhaar-based flow when a transaction_id is supplied.

I need to decide whether to reuse an existing Aadhaar ciphertext from a prior login transaction, or require and encrypt a freshly provided 12-digit Aadhaar value. There's a subtlety: should raw Aadhaar input be allowed to kick off account creation directly, bypassing the usual login-first lookup path? The underlying principle seems to be that the lookup must always run first, even when the desk suspects no ABHA exists for that mobile — so I shouldn't skip the Aadhaar lookup just because the mobile login already failed.

I'm also noting that running an Aadhaar login lookup first is effectively free when no account exists (the login attempt is rejected immediately before any OTP goes out), while if an account does exist, an OTP is triggered so the person logs into their existing account instead of accidentally creating a duplicate. And even enrollment by Aadhaar itself guards against duplicates by returning the existing linked account rather than creating a new one, though that shows up as a specific error screen — so I need to make sure the flow enforces checking first rather than relying on that fallback.

Now I'm working out the actual flow: creation should only be permitted from a transaction where the Aadhaar login lookup already came back empty, which means the backend needs to track that state and reuse the resulting ciphertext for account creation. The UI path for an unrecognized mobile number would prompt for Aadhaar, attempt a login lookup, and only proceed to creation (after consent) if no account is found — otherwise it falls back to OTP login for the existing account. But then I catch a requirement that complicates the ordering: the published consent text needs to be shown *before* asking for the Aadhaar number at all, which means I need to rearrange where the consent step sits in this sequence.

Neither PHR call needs `X-CM-ID`—only `X-token` is required for the profile call. Before designing the creation endpoints, I need to resolve the tension between "consent before Aadhaar is asked" and "search first," so I'll review the design's consent and suggested-journey sections.

result.content:
A wrong padding or digest does not fail when you encrypt. It fails at the API as a validation refusal that names the business field, which reads as a wrong Aadhaar or mobile number. Check the padding, the digest and the key before you doubt the plaintext. A stale cached certificate fails every encrypted call at once. ## The terms and conditions a person agrees to before an ABHA is created ### In plain words Before your system sends a person's Aadhaar number, show them the terms and conditions below and collect their agreement, through an "I agree" checkbox or another form of signature. Keep a record that they agreed. Every journey that creates an ABHA from Aadhaar starts here, and functional testing checks it in [CRT_ABHA_102](/docs/hiecm/v3/resources/test-cases/m1#crt_abha_102). Show the text exactly as written:
**Terms and Conditions** I, hereby declare that I am voluntarily sharing my Aadhaar number and demographic information issued by UIDAI, with National Health Authority (NHA) for the sole purpose of creation of ABHA number. I understand that my ABHA number can be used and shared for purposes as may be notified by ABDM from time to time including provision of healthcare services. Further, I am aware that my personal identifiable information (Name, Address, Age, Date of Birth, Gender and Photograph) may be made available to the entities working in the National Digital Health Ecosystem (NDHE) which inter alia includes stakeholders and entities such as healthcare professionals (e.g. doctors), facilities (e.g. hospitals, laboratories) and data fiduciaries (e.g. health programmes), which are registered with or linked to the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM), and various processes there under. I authorize NHA to use my Aadhaar number for performing Aadhaar based authentication with UIDAI as per the provisions of the Aadhaar (Targeted Delivery of Financial and other Subsidies, Benefits and Services) Act, 2016 for the aforesaid purpose. I understand that UIDAI will share my e-KYC details, or response of “Yes” with NHA upon successful authentication. I have been duly informed about the option of using other IDs apart from Aadhaar; however, I consciously choose to use Aadhaar number for the purpose of availing benefits across the NDHE. I am aware that my personal identifiable information excluding Aadhaar number / VID number can be used and shared for purposes as mentioned above. I reserve the right to revoke the given consent at any point of time as per provisions of Aadhaar Act and Regulations.
The `consent` block in the `enrol/byAadhaar` request records the agreement: `code` is `abha-enrollment` and `version` is `1.4`. Offering the text in other languages is optional. ### What happens Display the text verbatim, require an explicit "I agree" before the OTP request is sent, and store who agreed and when. Send the `consent` block with `code` `abha-enrollment` and `version` `1.4` in `enrol/byAadhaar`. ### How you know it worked The OTP request cannot be sent until the person has agreed, and your records show the agreement for every ABHA your system created. ### When it goes wrong A creation flow that sends the Aadhaar number before consent is collected fails functional testing at CRT_ABHA_102, whatever the API returns. ## A suggested ABHA journey, and what holds if you design your own ### In plain words A front desk adopts ABHA because the receptionist stops typing. A verified ABHA profile already carries the name, date of birth, gender, mobile, address and photograph. So the ABHA step comes before your registration form, and fills it. The suggested journey, in five steps: 1. **Start registering the patient** in your own system, under your own number. 2. **Ask whether they have an ABHA.** No means the form is typed by hand, and the patient is treated exactly the same. 3. **Take one identifier.** Aadhaar is the one to recommend, because it is the only route that ends in a KYC verified ABHA number. Mobile sits beside it. Under Aadhaar only, ask how they prove it: an OTP, a face scan, or a fingerprint or iris reader. 4. **Log in or create, decided by the answer.** Every identifier starts on the login path. One account signs the person in. Several need a chooser. None offers creation. 5. **Fill your form from what came back,** and let the receptionist confirm it rather than type it. Whatever journey you build, these hold: - **Look before you create.** Creating an ABHA for a person who already holds one leaves them with two ABHA numbers, and nothing in M1 merges them. - **The login token is not the profile token.** Login verify returns a short lived token, which the verify user call exchanges for the `X-token` that profile calls accept. - **An ABHA is optional to your record.** ABDM does not require a person to hold an ABHA to be treated. A journey that cannot finish without one blocks care. - **The profile is what ABDM holds**, not what is in front of your clinician. Present the filled form for confirmation rather than saving it unseen. ### What happens Send every identifier, Aadhaar included, to the login OTP request first, never straight to enrolment. Read `accounts` on the verify response: one account, call verify user with its `ABHANumber` and the same `txnId`; several, show a chooser and do the same with the chosen one; none, offer creation. data.reasoningText:
I'm writing the client module for the ABDM gateway, making sure sensitive values like Aadhaar, mobile, and OTP are encrypted before leaving the process and that nothing sensitive gets logged, only request identifiers.

Defining padding scheme...

I'm defining a custom exception class for ABDM errors that carries status, message, code, field, and request ID, plus a helper method to check if the error matches specific gateway codes.

Now I'm setting up default human-readable messages for each HTTP status code ABDM might return, with a fallback for server errors, and starting a normalization step that identifies non-field keys to filter out of error responses.

I'm reasoning through how field-keyed errors like txnId should only apply in error bodies, not success ones, and writing a helper that cleans up error codes by stripping trailing colons and whitespace.

Now I'm drafting a normaliser function that extracts code, message, and field from whatever error shape ABDM returns — handling lists by picking the first truthy item, plain strings as fallback messages (while being cautious about accidentally accepting HTML), and falling back to a default message when the payload isn't a usable dict. When there's a nested "error" dict, I pull the code and message from it.

I'm also handling flatter payloads where "code" or "message" appear directly, or where "error" is itself just a string like a routing failure ("Not Found" with a path/status). As a last resort, I scan remaining keys for any string value to use as the message, skipping metadata fields like timestamp, path, and status, and default otherwise. I'm second-guessing whether "Not Found" is a good enough message for that routing-failure case, but it seems acceptable for now.

Now I'm moving on to defining a response dataclass with status, data, content, content_type, and request_id fields, plus a helper that generates a UTC timestamp formatted with millisecond precision and a "Z" suffix.

Still writing request setup...

I'm second-guessing the Accept header, considering leaving it unset for endpoints like card downloads, then continuing to build the headers with content-type, bearer token, and merging any extra headers, before wrapping the actual HTTP call in a try block to catch request exceptions.

On failure, I log a warning and raise a 503 AbdmError so the caller gets a clean message rather than a raw exception. For parsing the response, I realize I need to be careful: the card endpoint returns image/png so it shouldn't be JSON-parsed, so I'm checking the content type and only skipping parsing when it starts with "image/", parsing JSON otherwise.

I log the response status, then handle error status codes by normalizing them into a code, message, and field. If it's a 401 with a known gateway credential error code, I invalidate the cached session token so the next call fetches a fresh one, since credential failures should be backed off from rather than retried immediately. I log the error details and raise an AbdmError reflecting the status.

Now I'm checking whether the gateway session request itself needs to call ensure_configured and get_session_token, noting that it uses `authenticated=False`. For ensure_configured, I verify ABDM is enabled with both client ID and secret set, otherwise raising a 503 error indicating ABDM isn't configured on the server. Then I start writing the session token retrieval function, checking the cache first.

Writing session token fetch logic...

If expiresIn is missing I'd rather not cache than guess wrong, though sandbox typically returns ~1200s with my 120s margin being safe. I'm considering decoding the JWT's `exp` claim as a fallback TTL source when expiresIn isn't present, so I'll add a lightweight base64url decoder for the payload without signature verification, then move on to implementing the certificate retrieval function.

For the certificate, I'm writing logic that checks the cache first, then fetches from ABDM's public certificate endpoint if missing, extracting the public key and encryption algorithm from the response and raising an AbdmError if either is absent or if the algorithm isn't one of the recognized encryption paddings.

I'm validating the public key before caching it, then storing the certificate for future use. For loading the key itself, I'm handling both PEM and DER formats, trying to parse PEM directly if the text starts with the expected header, otherwise decoding it as base64 DER, and catching parsing errors appropriately.

Now I'm writing the encryption function that fetches the cached certificate, loads its public key, and encrypts the value using the padding scheme matching the certificate's algorithm, returning base64-encoded ciphertext. I should also catch `UnsupportedAlgorithm` from the cryptography library for unexpected key types, since `binascii.Error` is already covered as a `ValueError` subclass.

I'm adding small helper functions for building ABHA URLs and formatting bearer tokens, then moving into abha.py where I'm defining one thin function per ABHA operation CARE needs for its M1 journeys, starting with constants for OTP systems and a login profile mapping keyed by identifier and OTP system type.

Adding helper functions for extracting response data and building OTP auth payloads, plus a check that raises an error on the "otpValue" field if the authResult indicates failure.

Adding more API functions...

Still defining enrollment endpoints...

Adding more API functions...

I'm also verifying the mobile OTP verification response shape, checking whether the auth result includes a transaction token that I need to carry forward.

I'm noting that the TRANSACTION_ID header uses an underscore, which some proxies strip but ABDM's spec requires it, so I'll leave it as-is. Now I'm writing a helper to normalize ABHA numbers by stripping non-digit characters and validating the length.

I'm also adding helpers for ABHA address normalization—lowercasing and appending the default suffix if missing, plus a function to strip the suffix—since ABHA addresses are case-insensitive and ABDM typically returns them lowercase.

Now I'm mapping the profile fields returned by the `/v3/profile/account` source, which includes ABHA number, preferred address, name components, date of birth parts, gender, mobile, address, district, state, pincode, and KYC verification status.

I'm comparing this against the PHR profile source, the enrollment ABHAProfile source, and the login accounts entry — each has slightly different field names and shapes (fullName vs separate name parts, dob vs day/month/year, kycStatus vs kycVerified, phrAddress arrays, etc.) that I need to reconcile into a single normalized schema.

Writing the normalization logic...

Finishing more fields...

Now I'm considering date format inconsistencies—ABDM sources use "DD-MM-YYYY" for accounts and enrollment profiles, but PHR's dateOfBirth field may follow a different convention, so I need to handle that variance carefully.

I'm planning a robust parser that prioritizes separate day/month/year string fields when available, falls back to trying multiple date string formats, and defaults to year-only if that's all that's given. For gender, I'm noting ABDM's single-letter codes and need to figure out how these map to CARE's gender choices, which I'll verify later—I also need to account for how the photo field arrives as base64-encoded data.

Now I'm designing the server-side transaction model that keeps ABDM's own tokens and encrypted identifiers cached under a TTL, so the browser only ever sees an opaque transaction id while everything sensitive stays server-side.

Still defining transaction fields...

I'm also noting that the transaction retrieval needs to raise an expired-session error if the cache lookup fails, and must not reveal whether a transaction belongs to another user—just return a generic not-found error instead. I should validate that transaction_id is a proper UUID to prevent cache key injection, then move into defining the identifier system constants for ABHA numbers and addresses.

I'm flagging a subtle bug: BasePatientIdentifierConfig's CACHED_CONFIG dict is a shared class attribute across subclasses, which could cause stale config rows to linger between tests—if a config row gets rolled back but the cache still holds the old instance, a PatientIdentifier could end up pointing to a config FK that no longer exists.

<technical_details>
**Environment and repo rules**

Frontend worktree:
- Path: `/Users/jacob/copilot-worktrees/care_fe/jacobjeevan-upgraded-happiness`, branch `jacobjeevan-abdm-m1-flows`. Never touch `/Users/jacob/Desktop/care_fe`.

Backend worktree:
- Path: `/Users/jacob/copilot-worktrees/care/jacobjeevan-abdm-m1-flows`, branch `jacobjeevan-abdm-m1-flows`, from upstream/develop.
- venv python: `/Users/jacob/Desktop/care/.venv/bin/python`.
- Tests: `DJANGO_SETTINGS_MODULE=config.settings.test <python> manage.py test care.abdm --keepdb`. Postgres and Redis are running. The test cache is Redis with `IGNORE_EXCEPTIONS` and `KEY_PREFIX` "test_", so clear the abdm cache keys in setUp.
- Never commit in `/Users/jacob/Desktop/care`, and never read the branches `abdm-m1-abha-flows` or `jacobjeevan-abdm-m1-core-backend`.

Credentials:
- The main checkout `.env` holds `ABDM_CLIENT_ID=SBXID_035123`, `ABDM_CLIENT_SECRET` (never print it), `ABDM_GATEWAY_URL=https://dev.abdm.gov.in`, `ABDM_ABHA_URL=https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api` and `ABDM_CM_ID=sbx`.
- The `.env` is read only when `DJANGO_READ_DOT_ENV_FILE=true`.

Commits:
- Use the trailer `Co-authored-by: Copilot App <223556219+Copilot@users.noreply.github.com>`.

**Backend patterns found**

Settings:
- `config/settings/config.py` is imported via `from .config import *` at the top of base.py, BEFORE base.py reads `.env` (line ~32).
- So the ABDM settings must go at the END of `config/settings/base.py`, where `env` reads `.env` values.
- Planned settings:
  - `ABDM_CLIENT_ID`, `ABDM_CLIENT_SECRET` (default "")
  - `ABDM_ENABLED = env.bool(default=bool(id and secret))`
  - `ABDM_GATEWAY_URL` (default `https://dev.abdm.gov.in`)
  - `ABDM_ABHA_URL` (default `https://abhasbx.abdm.gov.in/abha/api`)
  - `ABDM_CM_ID` (default "sbx")
  - `ABDM_ABHA_ADDRESS_SUFFIX` (default CM_ID)
  - `ABDM_REQUEST_TIMEOUT` (int, default 30)
- Add `"care.abdm"` to `LOCAL_APPS` (base.py ~134-140).

Router:
- `config/api_router.py` uses `router = DefaultRouter() if settings.DEBUG else SimpleRouter()`.
- Add the import and `router.register("abdm/abha", AbhaViewSet, basename="abdm-abha")`, e.g. near the `otp/patient` registration (~line 130).
- Patient is registered at line 432.

EMRBaseViewSet (`care/emr/api/viewsets/base.py` ~308) extends GenericViewSet; `get_exception_handler` returns `emr_exception_handler`, which behaves like this:

| Raised | Response |
|---|---|
| pydantic ValidationError | 400 `{"errors":[...]}` |
| DRF ValidationError with a dict containing "errors" | passed through |
| list or string | `{"errors":[{"type":"validation_error","msg"}]}` |
| Http404 | 404 |

Authorization and permissions:
- Call `AuthorizationController.call("can_create_patient", user)`, `call("can_write_patient_obj", user, patient)` and `call("can_view_patient_obj", ...)`. All return True for superusers.
- `can_write_patient_obj` checks `PATIENT_GLOBAL_EDIT_ACCESS_ENABLED` (default False), else roles via the patient's organization_cache or encounters.
- Permission slugs: `PatientPermissions.can_create_patient.name`, `can_write_patient.name` (`care.security.permissions.patient`).

Test helpers (`care/utils/tests/base.py` CareAPITestBase):
- `create_user`, `create_super_user`, `create_organization(org_type="govt")`, `create_role_with_permissions([...])`, `attach_role_organization_user(org, user, role)`, `create_patient(**kwargs)` (baker), `create_facility(user)`.
- Use `self.client.force_authenticate(user=user)` and `reverse("abdm-abha-...")`.
- Patient create tests call `PatientCreateLock().release()`.

Identifiers:
- System auto_maintained configs follow `care/emr/signals/patient/base.py`.
- Do NOT use the process-level `CACHED_CONFIG`; query `PatientIdentifierConfig.objects.filter(config__system=..., facility__isnull=True).first()`, else create with `IdentifierConfig(use=secondary, system, required=False, unique=False, regex="", display, auto_maintained=True, retrieve_config=PatientIdentifierRetrieveConfig(retrieve_with_year_of_birth=True, retrieve_partial_search=False)).model_dump(mode="json")`, status active. Imports come from `care.emr.resources.patient_identifier.spec`.
- After writing identifiers, call `patient.build_instance_identifiers(); patient.save()`.
- The generic patient create/update skips auto_maintained identifiers. Search works through the existing partial/YOB flow.

Dependencies:
- cryptography 49 is available (transitive, pinned in the lock). Don't edit the Pipfile. requests 2.33 and pydantic 2.12.

**Design decisions (final)**

Systems:
- `system.care.ohc.network/abha-number` (display "ABHA Number"), stored hyphenated `XX-XXXX-XXXX-XXXX`.
- `system.care.ohc.network/abha-address` (display "ABHA Address").
- Uniqueness is enforced in the link endpoint: one ABHA per patient and one patient per ABHA, naming the existing patient.

Consent (CRT_ABHA_102 vs search-first):
- The consent text (verbatim, design.md ~909-913) and an "I agree" checkbox gate the Aadhaar INPUT in the identify step.
- `login/send_otp` with identifier_type aadhaar requires `consent:{agreed:true, language}` and records `AbhaConsent` BEFORE sending.
- `create/send_otp` is allowed only from a transaction whose Aadhaar login lookup returned ABDM-1114. It reuses that ciphertext and consent, so the Aadhaar is never asked twice (VRFY_ABHA_403).
- A mobile lookup that hits 1114 tells the UI to switch to an Aadhaar lookup (consent first), keeping the mobile as the communication mobile.
- Creation by mobile is refused by name.

Token rule:
- If verify returns `refreshToken`, the token is the X-token; use it directly with no verify/user call.
- Otherwise it's a T-token and MUST be exchanged via verify/user. With 1 account, auto-exchange; with several, show the chooser; with 0, return not_found.
- Never branch on the account count when refreshToken is present.

Reading responses:
- Read `authResult`: verify calls can return HTTP 200 with `authResult:"failed"` and `message` (e.g. "OTP expired, please try again"). Treat that as an error with field "otp".
- A wrong OTP on profile login returns 400 with field-keyed `{otpValue:"..."}`. On byAadhaar, a wrong OTP is 422 ABDM-1204.

`mobile_verification_required`:
- byAadhaar's `ABHAProfile.mobile` may be masked ("******0903").
- Rule: required if the profile mobile is empty. Otherwise compare digits: with 10 or more digits, compare the last 10; else require that the given mobile ends with the profile's trailing digits.
- Still an assumption to confirm in the sandbox (CRT_ABHA_108/109).

Other decisions:
- The byAadhaar `BENEFIT_NAME` header is optional (benefit programmes only); omit it. The response can also have a legacy shape (`healthIdNumber`, `jwtResponse`); handle it as a fallback.
- PHR request OTP takes no txnId, so its resend is a fresh request. Profile login and enrolment resends pass the previous `txnId`. Resend limits: max 2, 60s cooldown, enforced server-side.
- First enrol request-otp sends `txnId: ""`.
- No callbacks; scan-and-register is out of scope.

**Planned backend modules (care/abdm)**

`apps.py`:
- `name="care.abdm"`, label "abdm".

`models.py`:
- `AbhaConsent(EMRBaseModel)`: facility FK (nullable), code "abha-enrollment", version "1.4", language, abha_number (blank), patient FK (nullable).
- Then run `makemigrations abdm`.

`client.py`:
- `AbdmError(status, code, message, field, request_id)`.
- `normalise_error`:
  - `{error:{code,message}}`
  - `{error:"str", path, status}`
  - top-level `{code, message, description}`
  - list `[{code:"ABDM-1006: ", message}]`, taking the first entry
  - field-keyed `{otpValue:"...", timestamp}`, skipping the timestamp, path and status keys
  - empty or non-JSON bodies, using a status-based default message and never showing raw HTML
  - strip a trailing ": " from codes
- `_timestamp()` returns UTC ISO with milliseconds and Z. Headers per call: REQUEST-ID (uuid4), TIMESTAMP, Content-Type and Accept.
- `_send`:
  - Log only REQUEST-ID, method, path and status.
  - A `requests.RequestException` becomes AbdmError 503.
  - On a 401 with code 900901 or 900902, delete the cached session token and do NOT retry (back off).
  - Treat any 2xx as success (202 for sessions and the PHR card).
  - Return `AbdmResponse(status_code, data, content, content_type, request_id)`.
- `get_session_token()`:
  - `POST {GATEWAY}/api/hiecm/gateway/v3/sessions` with header `X-CM-ID` and body `{clientId, clientSecret, grantType:"client_credentials"}`.
  - Cache under `abdm:gateway:session_token` with TTL `expiresIn - 60`.
- `get_public_certificate()`:
  - `GET {ABHA}/v3/profile/public/certificate`, sent with the bearer token.
  - Validate the algorithm name before caching it (6h, key `abdm:abha:public_certificate`).
  - Known algorithms: `RSA/ECB/OAEPWithSHA-1AndMGF1Padding` → OAEP(MGF1(SHA1), SHA1); `RSA/ECB/PKCS1Padding` → PKCS1v15. Refuse any other.
  - The key is base64 DER SPKI (handle PEM too; strip whitespace).
- `encrypt(value)` returns base64.

`abha.py`, one function per operation:
- Login scopes table:

  | Identifier | otp_system | scope | loginHint |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | aadhaar | aadhaar | `["abha-login","aadhaar-verify"]` | aadhaar |
  | mobile | abdm | `["abha-login","mobile-verify"]` | mobile |
  | abha_number | aadhaar | `["abha-login","aadhaar-verify"]` | abha-number |
  | abha_number | abdm | `["abha-login","mobile-verify"]` | abha-number |

- Profile login:
  - `login_request_otp`: `/v3/profile/login/request/otp`.
  - `login_verify`: `/v3/profile/login/verify` with body `{scope, authData:{authMethods:["otp"], otp:{txnId, otpValue: enc}}}`.
  - `login_verify_user`: `/v3/profile/login/verify/user` with header `T-token: Bearer <t>` and body `{ABHANumber, txnId}`.
- PHR (ABHA address) family:
  - `phr_search`: `/v3/phr/web/login/abha/search` with `{abhaAddress: full@suffix}`. ABDM-1211 means not found.
  - `phr_login_request_otp`: `/v3/phr/web/login/abha/request/otp` with scope `["abha-address-login","aadhaar-verify"|"mobile-verify"]`, loginHint "abha-address", loginId = the encrypted ABHA address, otpSystem aadhaar|abdm.
  - `phr_login_verify`: `/v3/phr/web/login/abha/verify` returns `{authResult, message, tokens:{token, refreshToken, expiresIn}, users:[{abhaAddress, abhaNumber, fullName, kycStatus, profilePhoto, status}]}`; `tokens.token` is the X-token.
  - `phr_profile`: `GET /v3/phr/web/login/profile/abha-profile` with X-token.
  - `phr_card`: `GET /v3/phr/web/login/profile/abha/phr-card`, 202 IMAGE/PNG.
- Enrolment:
  - `enrol_request_otp`: `/v3/enrollment/request/otp` with `{txnId, scope:["abha-enrol"], loginHint:"aadhaar", loginId, otpSystem:"aadhaar"}`.
  - `enrol_by_aadhaar`: `/v3/enrollment/enrol/byAadhaar` with `{authData:{authMethods:["otp"], otp:{txnId, otpValue: enc, mobile: plain}}, consent:{code:"abha-enrollment", version:"1.4"}}`. Returns `{message, isNew, txnId, tokens:{token, refreshToken, expiresIn}, ABHAProfile{ABHANumber, firstName, middleName, lastName, dob, gender, mobile (masked), photo, phrAddress[], address, districtName, stateName, pinCode, abhaStatus}}`.
  - `enrol_request_mobile_otp`: scope `["abha-enrol","mobile-verify"]`, loginHint mobile, otpSystem abdm.
  - `enrol_verify_mobile`: `/v3/enrollment/auth/byAbdm` with `{scope, authData:{authMethods:["otp"], otp:{txnId, otpValue: enc}}}`.
  - `enrol_suggestions`: `GET /v3/enrollment/enrol/suggestion` with header `TRANSACTION_ID` → `{abhaAddressList, txnId}`. A bad txn returns 401 ABDM-1017.
  - `enrol_create_address`: `/v3/enrollment/enrol/abha-address` with `{txnId, abhaAddress (no suffix), preferred:1}` → `{healthIdNumber, preferredAbhaAddress, txnId}`.
- Account:
  - `profile_account`: `GET /v3/profile/account` with `X-token: Bearer <x>`.
  - `profile_card`: `GET /v3/profile/account/abha-card`, 200 image/png.

`transaction.py`:
- A pydantic model stored in the Django cache at `abdm:abha:txn:<uuid>` with a 30 minute TTL. The owner user_id is enforced.
- Fields:
  - identity and routing: id, user_id, flow (login|create), identifier_type, login_family (profile|phr), otp_system, scope
  - secrets held as ciphertext only: login_id (encrypted, never plaintext), aadhaar_ciphertext, aadhaar_not_found flag, mobile_ciphertext
  - ABDM progress: abdm_txn_id, pending_step (login|enrol|mobile_verify), otp_sent_at, resend_count
  - tokens: t_token, x_token, x_token_expires_at
  - results: accounts, abha_number, abha_address, profile, consent_id, verified, is_new
- Do not store the plain mobile; the UI sends it with `create/verify_otp`.

`identifiers.py`:
- `get_abha_number_config()` and `get_abha_address_config()`.
- `find_linked_patient(abha_number, abha_address)`.
- `link_abha_to_patient(patient, number, address)`, which refuses when another patient holds the ABHA or the patient already has a different ABHA.

`api/viewsets.py`, `AbhaViewSet` at `/api/v1/abdm/abha/`:
- Actions:
  - `GET status/` → `{enabled, abha_address_suffix}`
  - `POST login/send_otp/` with `{identifier_type, value, otp_system?, consent?}`
  - `POST login/verify_otp/` with `{transaction_id, otp}`
  - `POST login/verify_user/` with `{transaction_id, abha_number}`, which must be in txn.accounts
  - `POST abha_address/search/` → `{found:false}` on 1211, else `{found, abha_address, auth_methods (AADHAAR_OTP→aadhaar, MOBILE_OTP→abdm; filter others), name, masked_mobile, status}`
  - `POST create/send_otp/` with `{transaction_id}`
  - `POST create/verify_otp/` with `{transaction_id, otp, mobile}`
  - `POST create/send_mobile_otp/` with `{transaction_id, mobile?}`
  - `POST create/verify_mobile_otp/`
  - `GET create/address_suggestions/`
  - `POST create/address/`
  - `POST resend_otp/`
  - `GET profile/`
  - `GET card/` (PNG passthrough)
  - `POST link/` with `{transaction_id, patient}`
- Responses return a journey state: `{transaction_id, step: otp|choose_account|not_found|mobile_verify|address|verified, identifier_type, message, masked_mobile, otp_system, resend:{remaining, available_at}, accounts, create_allowed, profile, linked_patient:{id,name}|null, is_new}`.
- Normalised profile: abha_number (hyphenated), abha_address, name, first, middle and last name, gender, date_of_birth, year_of_birth, mobile, address, district, state, pincode, photo, kyc_verified, status.
- Errors: AbdmError → `{"errors":[{"type":"abdm_error","code","msg","field"}]}`.
  - 4xx from ABDM maps to 400, except 503 when unreachable.
  - Return 503 or a validation error when ABDM is disabled.
  - ABDM-1114 on aadhaar/mobile/abha_number login, or 1211 on address, returns step not_found (create_allowed only for aadhaar).
- Permissions: `can_create_patient`, or `can_write_patient_obj` when a patient is given. Link requires `can_write_patient_obj`.

**Validation and UX rules**
- Aadhaar must be exactly 12 digits and mobile exactly 10 (CRT_ABHA_104, VRFY_ABHA_301/401), checked client-side and server-side before any call.
- ABHA number: 14 digits with or without hyphens.
- Address rules: length 8-18; letters and/or digits; at most one dot and one underscore, neither first nor last. Be lenient.
- One identify screen, titled for both outcomes; never ask "login or create?".
- Show the masked mobile from `message` ("OTP sent to ... ending with ******0903").
- Errors render inline on the active step, naming the field. Allow an OTP retry without re-entering the identifier.
- Name, DOB and gender are read-only while an ABHA is attached; address, mobile and email stay editable (CRT_ABHA_306).
- The account chooser lists name, number, address and photo, and says when an account is already linked to a CARE patient (VRFY_ABHA_303).

- Optional or not-run: CRT_ABHA_103/108, 115, 201-411, VRFY_ABHA_501/502, PROF_ABHA_601-605.

**Frontend patterns**
- API routes live in `src/types/<domain>/<domain>Api.ts` as `{path, method: HttpMethod.X, TRes: Type<T>(), TBody: Type<B>()} as const`.
- Calls go through `query()` / `mutate()`; `silent: true` suppresses the global toast. `HTTPError{status, cause}` carries errors.
- `getResponseBody` returns a Blob for image content types.
- The global errorHandler toasts pydantic-style `{errors:[{type,msg}]}` on 400.
- UI building blocks: `src/components/ui/input-otp.tsx`, dialog, sheet, card, radio-group, alert, badge and checkbox; icons from lucide-react.

- Whether `loginId` for an ABHA number should be hyphenated.
- The rule for `ABHAProfile.mobile` (masked or null) when the communication mobile differs.

### In plain words

The expensive failure in M1 is a person ending up with two ABHA numbers. Nothing
merges them, so the mistake is permanent and the patient carries it.

It is caused by journey decisions rather than by any single call. Four of them
matter.

### What happens

**Every identifier starts on the login path, Aadhaar included.** Wiring Aadhaar
straight to enrolment, because enrolment is where Aadhaar is most discussed,
sends everybody who already holds an ABHA to make a second one.

**`ABDM-1114` is the only answer that means nobody holds an ABHA.** A refusal
that names a field is not the same thing. A stale certificate reads back
identically, and creating an account on that is how the duplicate happens.

**Never ask the patient whether they want to log in or to create.** They often
cannot answer. One screen, titled for both outcomes, takes an identifier and
lets the response decide.

**Read the token, not the account count.** A verification that returns a
`refreshToken` has already returned the final user token, so use it. One without
a `refreshToken` is a short lived transfer token and must be exchanged at the
account selection call, whatever the length of the accounts array. Branching on
`accounts.length` sends the Aadhaar path into an exchange it must not make, and
the refusal then blames the token's shape rather than saying the call was
unnecessary.

Creation is from Aadhaar. ABDM publishes a mobile enrolment route, and an
account created that way is address only and never verified against a
government identity document. No later desk can look it up before spending a one
time password, and the person carries the lesser account permanently. Write that
rule into code as a guard that refuses an unknown method by name, because a rule
the code merely happens to satisfy is one that regresses silently.

When the desk already knows there is no ABHA, ask only for Aadhaar. Offering a
mobile there offers a path that cannot finish. The lookup still runs first: a
patient saying they have never had one is not evidence, and creating on somebody's
word is how the second number appears.

### How you know it worked

Run a login for an identifier nobody holds. You receive `404` with `ABDM-1114`,
no one time password is sent, and only then does the journey offer creation.

Run the Aadhaar login path. The verify response carries a `refreshToken`, the
journey uses it directly, and no exchange call is made. Run the mobile path and
the exchange call is made, because no `refreshToken` came back.

### When it goes wrong

- A login is refused with a message naming a field, and the journey offers
  creation anyway. Only `ABDM-1114` means nobody holds an account. Treat
  anything else as a failure to answer the question.
- The Aadhaar path is refused `Invalid T-token` at the account selection call.
  The journey branched on the account count instead of on `refreshToken`, and
  made a call it did not need to make.
- Two patients a week arrive holding two numbers. Something in the journey is
  creating before it has looked, and the lookup is the cheapest call available.

## Telling the truth on screen at the counter
